1:
Elijah arrives without a pedigree and the gap is handled differently. Henry observes that where a prophet usually enters with parentage and tribe, Elijah drops out of the clouds as if, like Melchisedek, without father or descent, which made some Jews fancy him an angel from heaven; but the apostle assures us he was a man of like passions, which Henry thinks may intimate not only the common infirmities but a temper hotter than most, fitting him for the daring sinners of his age: rough spirits are called to rough services, and the reformation needed such a man as Luther to break the ice. Clarke entertains the angel theory at greater length. Dismissing the apocryphal trifling about Elijah's birth and celibacy, he says one opinion bears more resemblance to truth than any: that he had no earthly parentage but was an angel united for a time to a human body; he even asks whether the name, which signifies he is my God, countenances a manifestation in the flesh of the Supreme Being, before conceding that the apostle's man of like passions is irreconcilable with it.

The Tishbite's home divides Gill from Ellicott. Gill prefers Kimchi's account, that he was first of a city called Toshab and afterwards dwelt in Gilead, identifying that city with the Thisbe in Naphtali. Ellicott takes the Greek reading, of Tishbe in Gilead, the last words added precisely to distinguish it from the Naphtali Tishbe, whose mention he thinks textually doubtful; the word rendered inhabitants properly means sojourners and shares a derivation with Tishbite, while the only alternative, the stranger of the strangers of Gilead, is doubtful Hebrew.

Why Elijah had to hide produces a clean split. Gill and Clarke give the obvious answer, that he was in danger from Ahab and Jezebel, Clarke adding that on the first drought Ahab would have sought his life. Henry and Delitzsch both reject it. Henry says concealment was intended not so much for his preservation, since it does not appear Ahab immediately sought him, as for a judgment on the people, who would have been blessed by his instruction and intercession, God appointing him to abscond lest he be urged to revoke the sentence. Delitzsch says the same and quotes an older writer for it: since the prophet had said the rain would come at his word, how would they have urged him to order it to come. Where Cherith lay none will settle. Clarke reports both opinions, west near Samaria, or east because the command was to turn eastward; Delitzsch says the Hebrew means both to the east of and in the face of, so it cannot be determined; Ellicott guesses east, from the prophet's own Gilead.

The ravens draw the sharpest note in the chapter. Ellicott defends the plain rendering as that of almost all the ancient versions and of Josephus, and turns on those who alter the vowel points to read Arabs, or merchants, or the inhabitants of a city Orbi or the rock Oreb: these singularly prosaic interpretations arise from a desire to be rid of a strange miracle, and pay for it with a gross improbability, since regular sustenance by human hands could not have gone on under the king's jealous vigilance. Henry instead multiplies reasons why ravens: they are birds of prey likelier to take his meat than bring it, unclean by the law, carrion-feeders bringing wholesome food, neglectful of their own young, and themselves fed by special providence. Clarke notes a Greek manuscript and some fathers reading bread in the morning and flesh in the evening against all other versions, and calls this the first account of flesh at breakfast and supper. Gill thinks the source need not be inquired into, but passes on the Jewish guesses: from Ahab's table, or Jehoshaphat's, or, as probable as any, from the tables of the seven thousand who had not bowed the knee.
8:
That the refuge is a heathen city is what strikes them. Henry makes most of it: our Saviour notices it as an early indication of favour designed for the Gentiles, since many widows were in Israel and some would gladly have taken him in, yet he is sent to bless a city of Sidon and so becomes the first prophet of the Gentiles; Israel having corrupted themselves worse than the nations, their casting off is justly the riches of the world, and Elijah driven out by his countrymen turns to the Gentiles as the apostles were afterwards ordered to do. He presses the choice of Sidon, since the Baal-worship now the crying sin of Israel had lately come thence with Jezebel, a Sidonian, so that out of Sidon God calls the destroyer of that idolatry, and hides his prophet in his enemy's own country. Ellicott reads the clause about Zidon as emphatic for the same reason, a providence finding welcome in the native place of the prophet's deadliest foe. Gill takes it as a trial of Elijah's faith to be sent among Zidonians where Jezebel had an interest, and records that Kimchi denied the place was Gentile at all, reading the phrase as near to Zidon rather than belonging to it.

On the site they converge. Clarke puts it between Tyre and Sidon but nearer the latter, its present name Sarphan, and reports a traveller who found only a few houses on the mountain tops, supposing the old city stood in the plain below among ruins. Gill cites the same traveller and puts it three quarters of a mile from Sidon; Ellicott has it on the great coast-road. On whether the famine reached so far Ellicott offers two answers: it may have, one authority making it last a year in that country, or, since the country depended on Israel for supplies, the distress may have been only the reflex of the famine there.

Whether the widow already believed divides Gill from Ellicott. Gill takes her oath by the living God to show her a good woman, swearing by him only, and taking Elijah for a prophet. Ellicott reads the same words the other way: the phrase recognises Elijah as a prophet of the God of Israel, but thy God probably implies no acknowledgment of that God by the woman herself as yet, of the sort neighbouring heathen often yielded. Henry leaves it open and uses the doubt to measure the trial, asking what assurance she had that this stranger was a prophet or had warrant to speak in that name, when a hungry vagrant might easily impose on her; then he answers himself: great was her faith, and all things considered it exceeded that of the widow who cast in two mites. Clarke says only that it was putting her faith to an extraordinary trial.

On the vessels and the miracle each adds something. Clarke insists the barrel is an earthen jar, not a wooden vessel, since in the East corn and meal are kept so against the insects, and that cruse means a bottle. Ellicott calls the miracle doubly remarkable: first that God's higher laws of miracle, like the ordinary laws of providence, take in the supply of what we should think homely and trivial needs, the opposite of what expectation would suggest; next that it is a miracle of multiplication, virtual creation though not out of nothing, doing rapidly and directly what ordinary law does slowly and indirectly. Clarke and Gill each reach for a gospel parallel, Clarke to the water at Cana found wine as it was drawn, Gill to the loaves increasing while the disciples ate. Henry weighs the two and prefers the hidden one: the increase of this widow's faith was as great a work in the kingdom of grace as the increase of her oil in the kingdom of providence.
17:
Why the child died divides them. Clarke takes the mother at her word, that she is conscious of some secret sin forgotten or passed over too carelessly and supposes her son's life taken to punish it; it is mostly in adversity, he adds, that we consider our moral state. Henry agrees and generalises: when God removes our comforts he remembers our sins against us, perhaps the iniquities of our youth, so our sins are the death of our children, and he does it that we may remember and repent of them; he guesses her former worship of Baal may be in view, and reads the affliction as a thorn in the flesh lest she be lifted up. Delitzsch denies the premise. He grants that she discerned a punishment and supposed the man of God's presence had drawn it on her, and finds in that half-heathenish belief a mind susceptible to divine truth and conscious of sin, which the Lord could not refuse to aid; but the death was no punishment for particular sins, any more than the blindness of the man born blind, being a medium for the manifestation of the works of God. Gill will only say she spoke rashly, in her passion and agony, forgetting the benefits received.

Elijah's own complaint is read two ways. Ellicott hears presumption, calling it characteristic of the half-presumptuous impatience shown more fully two chapters later, and taking Elijah to imply that his own lot as an unprotected fugitive is so hard that his presence must have brought trouble on the house sheltering him. Henry hears humble pleading: Elijah urges the greatness of the affliction to a widow, God being the widow's God, and then his own concern, that if death follows him into the houses receiving him others will fear to entertain him.

The stretching on the child divides them again, and Ellicott names the view he rejects: to suppose it merely the use of natural means of reviving is to explain the whole description away. The idea is of a healing virtue attaching in measure to the prophets, as it belonged without measure to our Lord, though in their case the power is made conditional on prayer. Clarke holds precisely the view Ellicott refuses, that Elijah did it to communicate some warmth to the body and dispose it to receive the departed spirit. Henry takes a third way, that the act was to affect Elijah himself with the case and to signify what God does by grace in raising dead souls.

On what returned to the child Clarke argues with himself. At the prayer he says the soul here surely means no more than the breath; at the fulfilment he reverses, holding that the word generally means the immortal spirit, and that the expression is strong proof not only that an immaterial spirit exists in man but that it can exist separately from the body, lying in the midst of him like a spring at the centre of a machine. Henry reaches the same conclusion and credits Grotius with thinking God designed the miracle to intimate it. On her closing words Ellicott traces three stages of faith, from speaking of Jehovah from without as the Lord thy God, to recognising him as God, to accepting the word in the prophet's mouth as truth, which seems to express conversion; Delitzsch reads the same progress and calls Elijah the forerunner of him who raises all the dead. Clarke closes the chapter by reopening its beginning: against those who keep the ravens he urges that the bird is unclean and carrion-feeding, that the reading needs three miracles where God's way is the simplest means, and that the word may mean merchants, disputing Bochart's lexicography and answering his objection that traders would have betrayed the hiding place, since they might be bound by inspiration or be among the seven thousand.
